title: Delaware Declares August 15 India Day, Joining Growing Wave of US State Proclamations
excerpt: The First State becomes the latest to formally recognize India's Independence Day, reflecting the Indian American community's growing civic influence across the United States.
body:
• Delaware Governor Matthew Meyer has declared August 15, 2026, as India Day, joining Massachusetts, New York, and other states in formally recognizing India's Independence Day.
  • Delaware's Indian American Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez — the first person of color in the role — has been central to strengthening Indo-Delaware ties.
  • The New York State Senate separately adopted Resolution J1935 urging Governor Hochul to proclaim August 15 as India Independence Day statewide.
  • A resolution in the US House of Representatives seeks to designate August 15 as a national day of celebration honoring both democracies.

Delaware has officially declared August 15, 2026, as India Day, adding the First State to a rapidly growing roster of US states formally recognizing India's Independence Day through gubernatorial proclamations and legislative resolutions.

Governor Matthew Meyer's proclamation comes ahead of India's 80th Independence Day, and follows a string of similar gestures from Delaware's executive office this year — including proclamations for Holi in March and the International Day of Yoga on June 21.

A State With Deep Ties

Delaware's Indian American community, though smaller than those in New Jersey, California, or Texas, has built outsized civic influence in recent years. The state's Secretary of State, Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez, is the first person of color to hold the position. She was sworn in on January 28, 2025, and has been active in strengthening ties between Delaware and India's Consulate General in New York.

The Indian American Community of Delaware, working in partnership with the consulate, has organized a series of cultural events around August 15. The community group AIACPA held its annual India Day community fair on August 8 in the capital, while the Hindu Temple of Delaware in Hockessin has hosted an Independence Day parade and flag-hoisting for over a decade, regularly drawing local elected officials.

"We want to create some kind of community. We want to show people that all are welcome."

— Bal Kamireddy, India Day event organizer, Hindu Temple of Delaware

A National Trend

Delaware's declaration is part of a broader pattern. Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey proclaimed August 15 as India Day in the Commonwealth earlier this month. The New York State Senate adopted Resolution J1935 in June, urging Governor Kathy Hochul to make the same declaration statewide. During that debate, Senator John Liu called India "a model of democracy for actually a lot longer than our country."

At the federal level, Congressman Shri Thanedar — one of the first Indian Americans elected to Congress — has introduced resolutions in the House seeking to designate August 15 as a "National Day of Celebration of the World's Two Largest Democracies." While the resolution remains in committee, it reflects the growing legislative footprint of the Indian American community, which numbers over 4.4 million and includes growing numbers of elected officials at state and local levels.

Celebrations Across the Country

India Day events are taking place across the United States this weekend and through August 15. The 44th India Day Parade in New York City, organized by the Federation of Indian Associations, remains the largest such event outside India, drawing over 100,000 participants annually with performances, tableaux, and appearances by Bollywood celebrities and civic leaders. This year's event is scheduled for August 16.

The 15th India Day Parade USA in Hicksville, New York, will take place on August 23, marking the 80th anniversary of Indian independence. Sunnyvale, California, and San Jose are also hosting major community events on August 15, with flag-hoisting ceremonies, cultural performances, and food stalls.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, these proclamations carry weight beyond symbolism. State-level recognition of India Day normalizes the community's cultural presence and opens doors for civic participation. Delaware's case is especially striking: a small state with fewer than 30,000 Indian American residents has produced an Indian American Secretary of State and now formally celebrates the country's independence alongside Holi and Yoga Day.

The US State Department issued a statement last year calling the India-US relationship "consequential and far-reaching," noting shared commitments to innovation, technology, and a secure Indo-Pacific. That diplomatic language is increasingly matched by grassroots recognition at the state level — one proclamation at a time.
